title: Knowledge Check 4 - Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 - FlexCards. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: A consultant wants to build a reusable detail view that can be embedded in several parent cards. What is the correct design approach?
options: Build the detail into each parent card separately
Create a child FlexCard with an explicit, self-contained data contract that receives its context from the parent
Nest the child five levels deep
Give the child a hard-coded record
questions.explanation: A reusable child FlexCard should have an explicit, self-contained data contract and receive its context from the parent, so it can be embedded in multiple parents. Duplicating the detail in each parent defeats reuse, deep nesting multiplies fetches, and a hard-coded record makes the child unusable elsewhere.

questions.question: A parent card should show a summary and let the user drill into detail without leaving the page. Which pattern is the best fit?
options: A link that navigates to a separate page
A modal that hosts a child FlexCard showing the detail
A static text element
A child card with no data contract
questions.explanation: A modal that hosts a child FlexCard keeps the user in context while showing the detail, which is the drill-down pattern. A link navigates away, a text element shows no detail, and a child without a data contract has nothing to display.

questions.question: What is the main risk of nesting child FlexCards too deeply?
options: The cards become too reusable
The data fetches multiply and the data contract becomes hard to trace
The cards lose their styling
The parent cannot pass context
questions.explanation: Deep nesting multiplies data fetches and makes the data contract hard to trace, slowing the page and complicating maintenance. Reusability is a benefit, not a risk, and styling and context passing are not the primary problems with depth.

questions.question: A FlexCard should show a warning banner only when a case is past its due date. What is the correct implementation?
options: Always show the banner
Add a condition that shows the banner when the due date is past
Hide the banner with a static setting
Remove the banner element
questions.explanation: A condition that evaluates the due date and shows the banner only when it is past is the correct use of conditional rendering. Always showing it ignores the data, a static hide removes it entirely, and removing the element defeats the purpose.

questions.question: A condition on a FlexCard never seems to fire. What is the most likely cause?
options: The element is styled incorrectly
The data source does not return the field the condition depends on
The card is expanded by default
The card has too many actions
questions.explanation: A condition that never fires is usually because the data source does not return the field the condition depends on, so the rule can never evaluate true. Styling, the expanded state, and the action count do not prevent a condition from firing.

questions.question: A consultant wants the same card to show different elements to a manager and an agent. What is the correct approach?
options: Maintain two separate card definitions
Use conditional rendering to show the relevant elements for each role
Show all elements to both roles
Remove the role distinction entirely
questions.explanation: Conditional rendering lets one card definition adapt to the role, showing the relevant elements for each. Two separate definitions duplicate logic, showing all elements to both buries what each needs, and removing the distinction ignores the requirement.

questions.question: A FlexCard should highlight a row when the user selects it. What should drive the highlight?
options: The data source
A state variable that tracks the selected row
Static JSON
A server refresh
questions.explanation: Selection is a transient interaction state, so a state variable that tracks the selected row should drive the highlight, updating in real time without a server round trip. The data source holds the record data, not the selection, and static JSON or a server refresh cannot respond to the click.

questions.question: What is the correct distinction between data and state in a FlexCard?
options: Data reflects the record; state reflects the user's current interaction
Data reflects the interaction; state reflects the record
They are the same thing
State is stored in the data source
questions.explanation: Data comes from the source and reflects the record, while state reflects the user's current interaction with the card. Confusing them leads to writing interaction state back to the source or failing to update on interaction. They are not the same, and state is not stored in the data source.

questions.question: A state variable is updated in many places and the card behaves unpredictably. What is the best fix?
options: Add more state variables
Define what each state variable means and which interaction changes it
Move all state into the data source
Remove conditional rendering
questions.explanation: A state variable with no clear owner or many updaters becomes unpredictable, so the fix is to define what each state variable means and which interaction changes it. Adding more variables compounds the problem, moving state into the source is wrong, and removing conditional rendering does not fix the state ownership.

questions.question: A card shows data for the specific record the user is viewing. What is the best placement?
options: A tab with no record anchor
A Lightning component on the record page
A utility panel
A dashboard with no context
questions.explanation: A card whose value depends on the record context belongs on the record page as a Lightning component, where it is bound to the record. A tab, utility panel, or dashboard has no record anchor, so the card would have to source its own context and would not automatically follow the record.

questions.question: A card shows cross-record aggregate data for managers. What is the best placement?
options: A Lightning component on a single record page
A tab that gives the card its own space
A console view for agents
A card bound to a case record
questions.explanation: Cross-record aggregate data is not anchored to one record, so a tab placement that gives the card its own space is best. A record-page component or a case-bound card would anchor it to a single record, and a console view is for task-driven agent work, not a manager's aggregate view.

questions.question: A service agent resolves cases in the console and needs a card that supports that task. What is the best placement?
options: A tab the agent rarely opens
A console view placement alongside the workspace
A dashboard for managers
A record page for a different object
questions.explanation: A task-driven card for an agent belongs in the console view, where the agent already works. A tab the agent rarely opens, a manager dashboard, or a record page for a different object would not put the card where the agent acts.

questions.question: A consultant is placing a card and has not yet defined the enablement goal. What should they do first?
options: Choose the placement that looks best
Define the goal in terms of the user's task, then place the card where that task happens
Place the card in every context
Skip the goal and rely on the card's design
questions.explanation: Placement strategy starts with the enablement goal: define what the user should do more easily, then place the card where that task happens. Choosing a placement without a goal is arbitrary, placing it everywhere is wasteful, and skipping the goal ignores the strategic purpose.

questions.question: A card is record-bound and needs the record anchor to show correct data. Which placement is consistent with its data needs?
options: A tab with no record anchor
A record-page component
A dashboard with no context
A utility panel
questions.explanation: A record-bound card needs the record anchor, which a record-page component provides. A tab, dashboard, or utility panel has no record anchor, so the card would have to source its own context and could not rely on the record.

questions.question: After rollout, a card placed to speed up case resolution is not helping agents. What should the consultant do?
options: Leave it and assume it works
Review whether the placement and the card support the goal, and adjust them
Remove all actions
Add more data to the card
questions.explanation: Placement is a hypothesis about where the user acts, so if the card is not helping the task, the consultant should review whether the placement and the card support the goal and adjust them. Leaving it assumes it works, removing actions or adding data does not address the placement problem.
